title: AVENIR-spatial-ate assess spatial scale of correlation

yaml.title: AVENIR-spatial-ate assess spatial scale of correlation
yaml.author: Ben Arnold (ben.arnold@ucsf.edu)

markdown.markdown:
Assess the spatial scale of correlation in mortality in AVENIR I in the Dosso region. The analysis is limited to Dosso randomization wave 1 to ensure sufficient person-time of observation (24 months) at each cluster location.

There are three main sections of the analysis. In each section, we repeated the analysis using data aggregated to the grappe level (community cluster, n=1389 with person-time at risk) and to the CSI health catchment level (n=160). The reason for repeating the analysis with data at the CSI level is that future monitoring in AVENIR-II is at the CSI level, and we wanted to assess whether aggregation introduces any artifact in our estimates of spatial scale of correlation. In short, it does not -- estimates are highly consistent in all analyses whether completed at the grappe or CSI level, in a setting with extremely high spatial density of data collection.

First, we estimate semivariance in mortality rates by different distances between clusters. We find that the range of spatial auto-correlation is approximately 30 km.

Second, we use a generalized linear model with Poisson distribution and Matérn spatial covariance to fit a spatial model of mortality. We find that a generalized krig model, which includes fixed effects for longitude and latitude slightly outperforms a simple krig model (intercept only). Under the MLE of the Matérn parameters, we find the spatial scale of correlation is below approximately 30-40 km, highly consistent with the semivariogram analysis.

Third, we try to explain the over-dispersion in mortality rates at different spatial scales. Overdispersion is defined in this context as variability beyond what we would expect under a Poisson distribution. To study this, we extend the Matérn spatial covariance model to include random effects for CSI (nested within district) and district. This allows us to partition the variance into fine-scale spatial process (Matérn covariance), CSI-level and district level. We find that the fine scale spatial process explains 97.5% of the extra-Poisson variation. Ignoring the spatial covariance, we find that CSI explains 72% of the variance. These results show that sources of extra-Poisson variability are at very fine spatial scales, below the CSI level. If the outcome were only measured at the CSI level, as in AVENIR-II, then CSI-level data would account for about 72% of the extra-Poisson variability.

The results imply that to identify highest mortality locations it would be necessary to measure mortality at very fine spatial scales, such as at the grappe- or CSI-level.

## Load data

```{r}

# load the AVENIR mortality
# data and GPS coordinates

  read_csv(here(final_data,"AVENIR_grappe_gps_2023-07-31.csv")) %>%
  rename(lat = median_latitude,
         lon = median_longitude)

grappe_phase_mort <- 
  readRDS(paste0(final_data,"AVENIR_grappe_phase_2023-07-31.rds"))


```

## Aggregate mortality to grappe and CSI levels

Sum person-time and deaths over the entire follow-up period.

Restrict to Dosso region grappes in randomization phase 1 because they have a full 24 months of follow-up. This ensures that we have sufficient information at each location. Grappes randomized at later times have far less information due to the shorter follow-up time of 6-12 months.

Additional aggregate mortality rates to the level of CSI. There are 160 CSIs represented in the original randomization.

```{r}
#| label: aggregate the mortality data to grappe and csi levels
#---------------------------
# aggregate mortality to
# grappe level
#---------------------------
grappe_mort <- 
  grappe_phase_mort %>%
  group_by(region, district,site_code, grappe,
           adaptive_rand, tx) %>%
  summarise(started_phase_1to59 = sum(started_phase_1to59, na.rm=T),
            pt_year_1to59 = sum(pt_year_1to59, na.rm=T),
            n_deaths_1to59 = sum(n_deaths_1to59, na.rm=T),
            n_alive_1to59 = sum(n_alive_1to59, na.rm=T),
            lost_1to59 = sum(lost_1to59, na.rm=T),
            
            started_phase_1to11 = sum(started_phase_1to11, na.rm=T),
            pt_year_1to11 = sum(pt_year_1to11, na.rm=T),
            n_deaths_1to11 = sum(n_deaths_1to11, na.rm=T),
            n_alive_1to11 = sum(n_alive_1to11, na.rm=T),
            lost_1to11 = sum(lost_1to11, na.rm=T),
            
            started_phase_12to59 = sum(started_phase_12to59, na.rm=T),
            pt_year_12to59 = sum(pt_year_12to59, na.rm=T),
            n_deaths_12to59 = sum(n_deaths_12to59, na.rm=T),
            n_alive_12to59 = sum(n_alive_12to59, na.rm=T),
            lost_12to59 = sum(lost_12to59, na.rm=T),
            
            deaths_per_1000_1to59 = n_deaths_1to59 * 1e3 / pt_year_1to59,
            deaths_per_1000_1to11 = n_deaths_1to11 * 1e3 / pt_year_1to11,
            deaths_per_1000_12to59 = n_deaths_12to59 * 1e3 / pt_year_12to59)

length(unique(grappe_phase_mort$site_code))
length(unique(d_gps$site_code))

#---------------------------
# join on GPS coordinates
# and CSI information
#---------------------------
d_mort <- grappe_mort %>%
  left_join(d_gps, join_by(region,district,grappe,site_code))

table(d_mort$region, d_mort$adaptive_rand)

# --------------------------------------------------
# Rename districts to match shapefile district names
# --------------------------------------------------
d_mort$district[d_mort$district=="Tibiri (Doutchi)"] <- "Tibiri"
d_mort$district[d_mort$district=="Illela"] <- "Illéla"


#---------------------------
# restrict grappe-level 
# data to Dosso rand 1
#---------------------------
d_grappe <- d_mort %>%
  filter(region == "Dosso" & adaptive_rand == "Random Allocation 1") %>%
  # drop a single grappe with zero person-time at risk
  filter(pt_year_1to59 > 0) %>%
  # create a log mortality rate variable
  mutate(
    log_deaths_per_1000_1to59 = ifelse(deaths_per_1000_1to59==0,log(0.1),log(deaths_per_1000_1to59))
  ) %>%
  # create factor variables for CSI and district for model fitting
  mutate(csif = factor(csi),
         districtf = factor(district)
         )


#---------------------------
# aggregate the data to the
# CSI level as well for
# sensitivity analyses at
# high level of spatial aggregation
#
# take median of lon/lat 
# coordinates across grappes
# as approximate locations of
# CSIs
#---------------------------
d_csi <- d_grappe %>%
  group_by(region, district, csi) %>% 
  summarise(pt_year_1to59 = sum(pt_year_1to59, na.rm=T),
            n_deaths_1to59 = sum(n_deaths_1to59, na.rm=T),
            lon = median(lon, na.rm=TRUE),
            lat = median(lat, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(deaths_per_1000_1to59 = n_deaths_1to59 * 1e3 / pt_year_1to59,
         log_deaths_per_1000_1to59 = ifelse(deaths_per_1000_1to59==0,log(0.1),log(deaths_per_1000_1to59))
         )

#---------------------------
# save temporary csv files
# for Tom

# write_csv(d_csi, file = here("results","avenir-1-mortality-dosso-csi-level.csv"))
```

## Estimate semivariograms

Semivariogram models assume the outcome is approximately normal. In the fits below, we use the log-transformed mortality rates at the grappe-level and CSI-level. Since a substantial number of grappes had zero events (close to 300), we exclude those grappes from the semivariogram model to ensure the outcome is close to normally distributed. We made no exclusions for the CSI-level model.

Estimates below suggest outcome correlation at very fine spatial scales below about 30 km regardless of level of aggregation of the data (grappe, CSI).

Later sections that include geostatistical model fits and partitioning of extra-Poisson variation in mortality at different spatial scales provide additional information about the relevant spatial scale of heterogeneity in the outcome. All results are highly consistent with one-another, suggesting the spatial scale in child mortality is below about 30-40 km, which is below the level of the CSI health catchment areas.

### semi-variogram, grappe level

```{r}
#| label: estimate semivariogram grappe level
#-------------------------------
# format grappe data as sf
#-------------------------------
d_grappe_sf <- st_as_sf(d_grappe, coords=c("lon","lat"), 
                 crs=4326) # set coordinate ref system to WGS1984


#-------------------------------
# estimate the semi-variogram
# at the grappe level
# for grappes with zero mortality
# omit from the analysis
#-------------------------------
d_grappe_sf2 <- d_grappe_sf %>%
  filter(deaths_per_1000_1to59>0)

library(gstat)
grappe_variogram <- gstat::variogram(log_deaths_per_1000_1to59 ~ 1, data=d_grappe_sf2)

grappe_var_mat <- gstat::fit.variogram(grappe_variogram, vgm(psill=NA,model="Mat",nugget=NA,kappa=1))
print(grappe_var_mat)


grappe_var_sph <- gstat::fit.variogram(grappe_variogram, vgm(psill=NA,model="Sph",nugget=NA))
print(grappe_var_sph)


# bind model fits into a single data frame for plotting
grappe_var_mat_preds <- variogramLine(grappe_var_mat, maxdist = 125)
grappe_var_sph_preds <- variogramLine(grappe_var_sph, maxdist = 125)
grappe_var_pred_data <- grappe_var_mat_preds %>%
  mutate(model = "Matern") %>%
  bind_rows(grappe_var_sph_preds) %>%
  mutate(model = ifelse(is.na(model),"Spherical",model))


plot_variogram_grappe <- ggplot(data = grappe_variogram, aes(x=dist,y=gamma)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data=grappe_var_pred_data, aes(x=dist,y=gamma, color=model)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cbpal[c(3,6)]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(0,140,by=20)) + 
  # scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(500,1000,by=100)) +
  # coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,130), xlim=c(0,125)) +
  labs(x="Distance (km)",y="Semi-variance") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.8,0.2)
  )

plot_variogram_grappe
```

## Fit geostatistical models

Below, we use geostatistical models to smooth outcomes and estimate the spatial scale of outcome correlation under a Matérn spatial covariance structure. Models fit to grappe level data and (aggregated) CSI-level data estimate a similar spatial scale of correlation, suggesting that there is a fundamental, fine-scale structure to the mortality rates in AVENIR-I that is not an artifact of data aggregation. We estimate high levels of correlation at spatial scales of less than about 20 km, and relatively low correlation at higher spatial scales.

In the next section, we will partition the exta-Poisson variability into different spatial scales to assess how much of the extra-Poisson variation in mortality is explained by district, CSI within district, and finally the fine-scale spatial field modeled here.

### krig, grappe-level data

Fit a geostatistical model to the grappe-level mortality data, assuming a Matérn spatial covariance structure. From the model fit, summarize correlation in mortality as a function of distance between grappes.

Below, will repeat for CSI-level aggregation.

```{r fit geostatistical model grappe}
#-------------------------
# identify available cores for
# parallel computing to speed up models
#-------------------------
avail_thr <- parallel::detectCores(logical=FALSE) - 1L 

#-------------------------
# generalized krig model
# linear terms for lat, lon
#-------------------------
fit_grappe_gen <- spaMM::fitme(n_deaths_1to59 ~ 
                                 1 + lat + lon + 
                                     Matern(1|lat + lon) +
                                     offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                                   data = d_grappe,
                                   family = poisson(link = "log"),
                               control.HLfit=list(NbThreads=max(avail_thr, 1L))
                               )

#-------------------------
# simple krig model
# intercept model
#-------------------------
fit_grappe <- spaMM::fitme(n_deaths_1to59 ~ 
                                 1 + Matern(1|lat + lon) +
                                    # (1|site_code) +
                                     offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                                   data = d_grappe,
                                   family = poisson(link = "log"),
                               control.HLfit=list(NbThreads=max(avail_thr, 1L))
                           )


# likelihood ratio test
# suggest generalized krig model better 
LRT(fit_grappe_gen,fit_grappe)

summary(fit_grappe_gen)

```

Plot correlation as a function of distance according to the model fit

```{r}
#| label: plot_matern_corr function

#--------------------------------------
# plot_matern_corr2()
#
# estimate the effect correlation by
# distance relationship given fitted
# Matern parameters in a geostatistical model
# of class HLfit from spaMM
#
# the model fit must have variables 
# "lon" and "lat" as the x,y coordinates
#--------------------------------------
plot_matern_corr2 <- function(spamm_model_fit, 
                             maxdist=100) {
  
  # create a distance matrix between all points
  # compute great circle distances in meters
  dist_mat_m <- spamm_model_fit$data %>%
    st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs=4326) %>%
    st_distance(which = "Great Circle") %>%
    as.numeric()
  
  model_dist_mat <- as.matrix(dist(spamm_model_fit$data [,c("lon","lat")]))
  
  # get estimated parameters from the Matern function
  est_nu <- spamm_model_fit$CorrEst_and_RanFix$corrPars$`1`$nu
  est_rho <- spamm_model_fit$CorrEst_and_RanFix$corrPars$`1`$rho
  # estimate the correlation between each location
  matern_cor <- MaternCorr(d = model_dist_mat, nu=est_nu, rho=est_rho)
  # store in a data frame for plotting
  d_matern_cor <- data.frame(
    distms = as.numeric(model_dist_mat),
    distkm = as.numeric(dist_mat_m)/1000,
    materncor = as.numeric(matern_cor)) %>%
    arrange(distms) %>%
    group_by(distkm) %>%
    slice(1) %>%
    ungroup()
  
  # there is a very, very slightly imperfect translation
  # between units in lat/lon used in the geostatistical
  # model and the actual great circle distances on earth
  # regress the two to get a very accurate estimate for plotting
  mskmfit <- lm(distkm~distms,data=d_matern_cor)
  d_matern_cor$pdistkm <- predict(mskmfit)
  
  #--------------------------------------
  # plot the correlation function
  #--------------------------------------
  plot_materncor <- ggplot(data = d_matern_cor %>% filter(pdistkm<=maxdist)) +
    # geom_point(aes(x=distms,y=distkm)) +
    geom_point(aes(x=pdistkm, y = materncor),color="black",alpha=1,size=0.1) + 
    # geom_vline(xintercept= 3 ,color="gray60", lwd=0.1) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0,1,by=0.2)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(0,maxdist,by=20)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,maxdist),ylim=c(0,1)) +
    labs(x="distance (km)",y = "Matern correlation") +
    annotate("text",x=15,y=0.9,label=paste("nu ==", deparse(sprintf("%1.1f",est_nu))),parse=TRUE, hjust =0, size=8)+
    annotate("text",x=15,y=0.7,label=paste("rho ==", deparse(sprintf("%1.1f",est_rho))),parse=TRUE, hjust =0, size=8)+
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
    )
  
  
  return(plot_materncor)
  
}
```

```{r}
#| label: plot outcome correlation as a function of grappe distance
#| 
(plot_corr_grappe <- plot_matern_corr2(spamm_model_fit=fit_grappe_gen, maxdist=125))
```

## Assess over-dispersion in outcomes

Below, we use a hierarchical mixed effects model to partition the variance in child mortality and assess contributions to extra-Poisson variation as a measure of overdispersion. In this section, I used GPT5o to embellish the annotation and explanation.

**1. Overdispersion in Poisson data**

**Overdispersion** means:

> The variance of the observed counts exceeds what is expected under the assumed sampling model (e.g., Poisson variance = mean).

**Random effects** in hierarchical models are *structured ways* to explain (and partition) that extra variance — i.e., to turn “unexplained overdispersion” into *explained* variation attributable to different spatial or grouping levels.

So the connection is:

> The proportion of total random-effect variance explained by each level ≈ the proportion of overdispersion attributable to clustering at that level.

In a simple Poisson model:

$Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \quad \text{Var}(Y_i) = \mu_i$

If the empirical variance is much larger than the mean, there is *extra-Poisson* variation (overdispersion). This extra variance can arise because the Poisson assumption of conditionally independent events with constant rate is violated — for example:

\- individuals or grappes have different underlying rates (heterogeneity),

\- events are clustered in space,

\- unobserved covariates vary by district, etc.

**2. Random effects as sources of structured overdispersion**

When we introduce random effects, we assume the rate parameter itself varies according to some distribution:

$\log(\mu*{ijk}) = \beta_0 + b_{\text{district}_j} + b_{\text{CSI}_{k(j)}} + s(lon,lat)$

where each random effect contributes a variance term on the latent (log) scale.

Then, marginally (after integrating over random effects):

$\text{Var}(Y_{ijk}) = E(Y_{ijk}) + \text{Var}_b[E(Y_{ijk}|b)]$.

The first term is the *Poisson variance*, and the second term is *extra-Poisson variance* due to heterogeneity in the random effects.

Hence, **random-effect variances are model-based measures of overdispersion** — they tell us how much extra variation is induced by each hierarchical level.

**3. Relating random-effect variance to overdispersion**

On the latent scale (log-link):

-   Each random effect adds variance $\lambda_\ell$ (for level $\ell$).

-   The total latent variance = sum of all random-effect variances (plus residual Poisson variance).

On the **observation scale** (counts):

-   These variances translate into multiplicative variability in rates.

-   For small variances, you can approximate:

$\text{Var}(Y) \approx \mu + \mu^2 \sum_\ell \lambda_\ell$

(a Taylor expansion, assuming the link is log and random effects are normal with variance $\lambda$).

So the “overdispersion factor”

$\phi = \frac{\text{Var}(Y)}{E(Y)} - 1$

is approximately $\mu \sum_\ell \lambda_\ell$, meaning each $\lambda$ term contributes additively to extra-Poisson variance.

Therefore:

> The relative size of $\lambda$ (district, CSI, sub-CSI spatial process) estimates the relative contribution to total overdispersion at each spatial scale.

**4. From variance partitioning to “overdispersion partitioning”**

From a hierarchical model estimate with variances of random effects $\lambda$ estimated on the log scale, we can express each level’s contribution to the extra-poisson variation (overdispersion) as: $\text{Proportion}_\ell = \frac{\lambda_\ell}{\sum \lambda_\ell}$​

**5. Analogy to Negative Binomial model**

A single-level random intercept Poisson model (with `(1|group)`) is mathematically equivalent to a Negative Binomial model where the random effect variance defines the NB overdispersion parameter $\theta$:

$\lambda_{NB} \approx \frac{1}{\theta}$

So we can think of each $\lambda_\ell$ in a hierarchical model as a component of that overdispersion. In other words, hierarchical Poisson + RE model = multi-level Negative Binomial, decomposing $\theta$ into structured sources.

```{r}
#| label: fit hierarchical spatial model to assess overdispersion
#---------------------------
# augment the Matern spatial
# model to include CSI and
# district level random effects
# then, partition the variance
# to see how much of the 
# variance in mortality is 
# explained by each level
#
# omit lon/lat fixed effects
# from the generalized krig model above
#---------------------------
fit_nested <- spaMM::fitme(n_deaths_1to59 ~ 
                             1 + 
                             # lon + lat +
                             Matern(1|lat + lon) +
                             (1 | districtf:csif) +
                             (1 | districtf) +
                             offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                           data = d_grappe,
                           family = poisson(link = "log"),
                           control.HLfit=list(NbThreads=max(avail_thr, 1L))
                           )

# extract the variance components from the model
varcomps <- get_ranPars(fit_nested)
varcomps$lambda
# summarize the proportion of the variance in mortality
# explained by each random effect
# (fine-scale spatial correlation, CSI within district, district)
prop_var <- varcomps$lambda / sum(varcomps$lambda)
round(prop_var,3)
```

These results suggest that the Matérn spatial correlation accounts for approximately 97.5% of the extra-Poisson variability, and that CSIs (within district) account for the remaining 2.5% of the extra-Poisson variability.

In the final model fit, below, we exclude the Matérn spatial covariance matrix from the random effects. If ignoring very fine-scale outcome correlation, CSI (within district) explains approximately 72% of the extra-Poisson variability and district explains the remaining 28%.

Together, these results show that much of the spatial correlation in mortality is very fine-scale, below the level of the CSI catchment areas. This is consistent with the geospatial model and the semivariogram results.

## Summary

Assess the spatial scale of correlation in mortality in AVENIR I in the Dosso region. The analysis is limited to Dosso randomization wave 1 to ensure sufficient person-time of observation (24 months) at each cluster location.

There are three main sections of the analysis. In each section, we repeated the analysis using data aggregated to the grappe level (community cluster, n=1389 with person-time at risk) and to the CSI health catchment level (n=160). The reason for repeating the analysis with data at the CSI level is that future monitoring in AVENIR-II is at the CSI level, and we wanted to assess whether aggregation introduces any artifact in our estimates of spatial scale of correlation. In short, it does not -- estimates are highly consistent in all analyses whether completed at the grappe or CSI level, in a setting with extremely high spatial density of data collection.

First, we estimate semivariance in mortality rates by different distances between clusters. We find that the range of spatial auto-correlation is approximately 30 km.

Second, we use a generalized linear model with Poisson distribution and Matérn spatial covariance to fit a spatial model of mortality. We find that a generalized krig model, which includes fixed effects for longitude and latitude slightly outperforms a simple krig model (intercept only). Under the MLE of the Matérn parameters, we find the spatial scale of correlation is below approximately 30-40 km, highly consistent with the semivariogram analysis.

Third, we try to explain the over-dispersion in mortality rates at different spatial scales. Overdispersion is defined in this context as variability beyond what we would expect under a Poisson distribution. To study this, we extend the Matérn spatial covariance model to include random effects for CSI (nested within district) and district. This allows us to partition the variance into fine-scale spatial process (Matérn covariance), CSI-level and district level. We find that the fine scale spatial process explains 97.5% of the extra-Poisson variation. Ignoring the spatial covariance, we find that CSI explains 72% of the variance. These results show that sources of extra-Poisson variability are at very fine spatial scales, below the CSI level. If the outcome were only measured at the CSI level, as in AVENIR-II, then CSI-level data would account for about 72% of the extra-Poisson variability.

The results imply that to identify highest mortality locations it would be necessary to measure mortality at very fine spatial scales, such as at the grappe- or CSI-level.

## Estimate semivariograms

Semivariogram models assume the outcome is approximately normal. In the fits below, we use the log-transformed mortality rates at the grappe-level and CSI-level. Since a substantial number of grappes had zero events (close to 300), we exclude those grappes from the semivariogram model to ensure the outcome is close to normally distributed. We made no exclusions for the CSI-level model.

Estimates below suggest outcome correlation at very fine spatial scales below about 30 km regardless of level of aggregation of the data (grappe, CSI).

Later sections that include geostatistical model fits and partitioning of extra-Poisson variation in mortality at different spatial scales provide additional information about the relevant spatial scale of heterogeneity in the outcome. All results are highly consistent with one-another, suggesting the spatial scale in child mortality is below about 30-40 km, which is below the level of the CSI health catchment areas.

## Fit geostatistical models

Below, we use geostatistical models to smooth outcomes and estimate the spatial scale of outcome correlation under a Matérn spatial covariance structure. Models fit to grappe level data and (aggregated) CSI-level data estimate a similar spatial scale of correlation, suggesting that there is a fundamental, fine-scale structure to the mortality rates in AVENIR-I that is not an artifact of data aggregation. We estimate high levels of correlation at spatial scales of less than about 20 km, and relatively low correlation at higher spatial scales.

In the next section, we will partition the exta-Poisson variability into different spatial scales to assess how much of the extra-Poisson variation in mortality is explained by district, CSI within district, and finally the fine-scale spatial field modeled here.

### krig, grappe-level data

Fit a geostatistical model to the grappe-level mortality data, assuming a Matérn spatial covariance structure. From the model fit, summarize correlation in mortality as a function of distance between grappes.

Below, will repeat for CSI-level aggregation.

```{r fit geostatistical model grappe}

# identify available cores for
# parallel computing to speed up models

avail_thr <- parallel::detectCores(logical=FALSE) - 1L 

#-------------------------
# generalized krig model
# linear terms for lat, lon

fit_grappe_gen <- spaMM::fitme(n_deaths_1to59 ~ 
                                 1 + lat + lon + 
                                     Matern(1|lat + lon) +
                                     offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                                   data = d_grappe,
                                   family = poisson(link = "log"),
                               control.HLfit=list(NbThreads=max(avail_thr, 1L))
                               )

#-------------------------
# simple krig model
# intercept model

fit_grappe <- spaMM::fitme(n_deaths_1to59 ~

                                    # (1|site_code) +
                                     offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
```

Plot correlation as a function of distance according to the model fit

```{r}
#| label: plot_matern_corr function

#--------------------------------------
# plot_matern_corr2()
#
# estimate the effect correlation by
# distance relationship given fitted
# Matern parameters in a geostatistical model
# of class HLfit from spaMM
#
# the model fit must have variables 
# "lon" and "lat" as the x,y coordinates
#--------------------------------------
plot_matern_corr2 <- function(spamm_model_fit, 
                             maxdist=100) {
  
  # create a distance matrix between all points
  # compute great circle distances in meters
  dist_mat_m <- spamm_model_fit$data %>%
    st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs=4326) %>%
    st_distance(which = "Great Circle") %>%
    as.numeric()
  
  model_dist_mat <- as.matrix(dist(spamm_model_fit$data [,c("lon","lat")]))
  
  # get estimated parameters from the Matern function
  est_nu <- spamm_model_fit$CorrEst_and_RanFix$corrPars$`1`$nu
  est_rho <- spamm_model_fit$CorrEst_and_RanFix$corrPars$`1`$rho
  # estimate the correlation between each location
  matern_cor <- MaternCorr(d = model_dist_mat, nu=est_nu, rho=est_rho)
  # store in a data frame for plotting
  d_matern_cor <- data.frame(
    distms = as.numeric(model_dist_mat),
    distkm = as.numeric(dist_mat_m)/1000,
    materncor = as.numeric(matern_cor)) %>%
    arrange(distms) %>%
    group_by(distkm) %>%
    slice(1) %>%
    ungroup()
  
  # there is a very, very slightly imperfect translation
  # between units in lat/lon used in the geostatistical
  # model and the actual great circle distances on earth
  # regress the two to get a very accurate estimate for plotting
  mskmfit <- lm(distkm~distms,data=d_matern_cor)
  d_matern_cor$pdistkm <- predict(mskmfit)
  
  #--------------------------------------
  # plot the correlation function
  #--------------------------------------
  plot_materncor <- ggplot(data = d_matern_cor %>% filter(pdistkm<=maxdist)) +
    # geom_point(aes(x=distms,y=distkm)) +
    geom_point(aes(x=pdistkm, y = materncor),color="black",alpha=1,size=0.1) + 
    # geom_vline(xintercept= 3 ,color="gray60", lwd=0.1) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0,1,by=0.2)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(0,maxdist,by=20)) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,maxdist),ylim=c(0,1)) +
    labs(x="distance (km)",y = "Matern correlation") +
    annotate("text",x=15,y=0.9,label=paste("nu ==", deparse(sprintf("%1.1f",est_nu))),parse=TRUE, hjust =0, size=8)+
    annotate("text",x=15,y=0.7,label=paste("rho ==", deparse(sprintf("%1.1f",est_rho))),parse=TRUE, hjust =0, size=8)+
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
    )
  
  
  return(plot_materncor)
  
}
```

```{r fit geostatistical model csi}
                                   data = d_csi,
                                   family = poisson(link = "log"),
                               control.HLfit=list(NbThreads=max(avail_thr, 1L))
                        )


# likelihood ratio test
# suggest generalized krig model better 
LRT(fit_csi_gen,fit_csi)

summary(fit_csi_gen)

```

## Assess over-dispersion in outcomes

Below, we use a hierarchical mixed effects model to partition the variance in child mortality and assess contributions to extra-Poisson variation as a measure of overdispersion. In this section, I used GPT5o to embellish the annotation and explanation.

**1. Overdispersion in Poisson data**

**Overdispersion** means:

> The variance of the observed counts exceeds what is expected under the assumed sampling model (e.g., Poisson variance = mean).

**Random effects** in hierarchical models are *structured ways* to explain (and partition) that extra variance — i.e., to turn “unexplained overdispersion” into *explained* variation attributable to different spatial or grouping levels.

So the connection is:

> The proportion of total random-effect variance explained by each level ≈ the proportion of overdispersion attributable to clustering at that level.

In a simple Poisson model:

$Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \quad \text{Var}(Y_i) = \mu_i$

If the empirical variance is much larger than the mean, there is *extra-Poisson* variation (overdispersion). This extra variance can arise because the Poisson assumption of conditionally independent events with constant rate is violated — for example:

\- individuals or grappes have different underlying rates (heterogeneity),

\- events are clustered in space,

\- unobserved covariates vary by district, etc.

**2. Random effects as sources of structured overdispersion**

When we introduce random effects, we assume the rate parameter itself varies according to some distribution:

$\log(\mu*{ijk}) = \beta_0 + b_{\text{district}_j} + b_{\text{CSI}_{k(j)}} + s(lon,lat)$

where each random effect contributes a variance term on the latent (log) scale.

Then, marginally (after integrating over random effects):

$\text{Var}(Y_{ijk}) = E(Y_{ijk}) + \text{Var}_b[E(Y_{ijk}|b)]$.

The first term is the *Poisson variance*, and the second term is *extra-Poisson variance* due to heterogeneity in the random effects.

Hence, **random-effect variances are model-based measures of overdispersion** — they tell us how much extra variation is induced by each hierarchical level.

**3. Relating random-effect variance to overdispersion**

On the latent scale (log-link):

-   Each random effect adds variance $\lambda_\ell$ (for level $\ell$).

-   The total latent variance = sum of all random-effect variances (plus residual Poisson variance).

On the **observation scale** (counts):

-   These variances translate into multiplicative variability in rates.

-   For small variances, you can approximate:

$\text{Var}(Y) \approx \mu + \mu^2 \sum_\ell \lambda_\ell$

(a Taylor expansion, assuming the link is log and random effects are normal with variance $\lambda$).

So the “overdispersion factor”

$\phi = \frac{\text{Var}(Y)}{E(Y)} - 1$

is approximately $\mu \sum_\ell \lambda_\ell$, meaning each $\lambda$ term contributes additively to extra-Poisson variance.

Therefore:

> The relative size of $\lambda$ (district, CSI, sub-CSI spatial process) estimates the relative contribution to total overdispersion at each spatial scale.

**4. From variance partitioning to “overdispersion partitioning”**

From a hierarchical model estimate with variances of random effects $\lambda$ estimated on the log scale, we can express each level’s contribution to the extra-poisson variation (overdispersion) as: $\text{Proportion}_\ell = \frac{\lambda_\ell}{\sum \lambda_\ell}$​

**5. Analogy to Negative Binomial model**

A single-level random intercept Poisson model (with `(1|group)`) is mathematically equivalent to a Negative Binomial model where the random effect variance defines the NB overdispersion parameter $\theta$:

$\lambda_{NB} \approx \frac{1}{\theta}$

So we can think of each $\lambda_\ell$ in a hierarchical model as a component of that overdispersion. In other words, hierarchical Poisson + RE model = multi-level Negative Binomial, decomposing $\theta$ into structured sources.

```{r}
#| label: fit hierarchical spatial model to assess overdispersion
#---------------------------
# augment the Matern spatial
# model to include CSI and
# district level random effects
# then, partition the variance
# to see how much of the 
# variance in mortality is 
# explained by each level
#
# omit lon/lat fixed effects
# from the generalized krig model above
#---------------------------
fit_nested <- spaMM::fitme(n_deaths_1to59 ~ 
                             1 + 
                             # lon + lat +
                             Matern(1|lat + lon) +
                             (1 | districtf:csif) +
                             (1 | districtf) +
                             offset(log(pt_year_1to59)),
                           data = d_grappe,
                           family = poisson(link = "log"),
                           control.HLfit=list(NbThreads=max(avail_thr, 1L))
                           )

# extract the variance components from the model
varcomps <- get_ranPars(fit_nested)
varcomps$lambda
# summarize the proportion of the variance in mortality
# explained by each random effect
# (fine-scale spatial correlation, CSI within district, district)
prop_var <- varcomps$lambda / sum(varcomps$lambda)
round(prop_var,3)
```

These results suggest that the Matérn spatial correlation accounts for approximately 97.5% of the extra-Poisson variability, and that CSIs (within district) account for the remaining 2.5% of the extra-Poisson variability.

In the final model fit, below, we exclude the Matérn spatial covariance matrix from the random effects. If ignoring very fine-scale outcome correlation, CSI (within district) explains approximately 72% of the extra-Poisson variability and district explains the remaining 28%.

Together, these results show that much of the spatial correlation in mortality is very fine-scale, below the level of the CSI catchment areas. This is consistent with the geospatial model and the semivariogram results.
